## The signal

The highlighted UC study found **RIBC2 promoter hypermethylation and reduced transcript abundance** [Kang et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5000688/).

::: {.gene-mechanism}
::: {.gene-state}
**RIBC2 present**

In vertebrate model work, Ribc2 localizes to motile-cilia axonemes and supports organized beating.
:::
::: {.gene-flow-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.gene-state .gene-state-off}
**Ribc2 disrupted**

Xenopus experiments showed disorganized axonemes and impaired ciliary beating.
:::
:::

The functional evidence comes from an [RFX2 ciliogenesis study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3889689/), not UC colon. The ordinary colonic surface epithelium is not a classic motile-ciliated tissue, so importing that phenotype directly would be misleading. RIBC2 may mark a cell population, have a different intracellular role, or be an epigenetic passenger here.

## If expression stops in this context

The answer remains unknown. Confirm which colonic cells express RIBC2, whether the protein is present, and whether promoter methylation explains within-cell repression. A methylation biomarker can be useful even when its encoded protein is not mechanistically central.

<details><summary><strong>Evidence boundary</strong></summary>

“Cilia-related in a vertebrate model” is supported. “RIBC2 loss damages the UC epithelial barrier” is not yet supported.
</details>
